verses.text: At that time, Judah went down from his brothers, and visited a certain Adullamite, whose name was Hirah.
Judah saw there a daughter of a certain Canaanite whose name was Shua. He took her, and went in to her.
She conceived, and bore a son; and he named him Er.
She conceived again, and bore a son; and she named him Onan.
She yet again bore a son, and named him Shelah: and he was at Chezib, when she bore him.
Judah took a wife for Er, his firstborn, and her name was Tamar.
Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked in Yahweh’s sight. Yahweh killed him.
Judah said to Onan, “Go in to your brother’s wife, and perform the duty of a husband’s brother to her, and raise up offspring  for your brother.”
Onan knew that the offspring  wouldn’t be his; and when he went in to his brother’s wife, he spilled it on the ground, lest he should give offspring  to his brother.
The thing which he did was evil in Yahweh’s sight, and he killed him also.

Then Judah said to Tamar, his daughter-in-law, “Remain a widow in your father’s house, until Shelah, my son, is grown up”; for he said, “Lest he also die, like his brothers.” Tamar went and lived in her father’s house.
After many days, Shua’s daughter, the wife of Judah, died. Judah was comforted, and went up to his sheep shearers to Timnah, he and his friend Hirah, the Adullamite.
Tamar was told, “Behold, your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep.”

She took off of her the garments of her widowhood, and covered herself with her veil, and wrapped herself, and sat in the gate of Enaim, which is by the way to Timnah; for she saw that Shelah was grown up, and she wasn’t given to him as a wife.
When Judah saw her, he thought that she was a prostitute, for she had covered her face.
He turned to her by the way, and said, “Please come, let me come in to you,” for he didn’t know that she was his daughter-in-law. She said, “What will you give me, that you may come in to me?”
He said, “I will send you a young goat from the flock.” She said, “Will you give me a pledge, until you send it?”
He said, “What pledge will I give you?” She said, “Your signet and your cord, and your staff that is in your hand.” He gave them to her, and came in to her, and she conceived by him.
She arose, and went away, and put off her veil from her, and put on the garments of her widowhood.
Judah sent the young goat by the hand of his friend, the Adullamite, to receive the pledge from the woman’s hand, but he didn’t find her.
Then he asked the men of her place, saying, “Where is the prostitute, that was at Enaim by the road?” They said, “There has been no prostitute here.”
He returned to Judah, and said, “I haven’t found her; and also the men of the place said, ‘There has been no prostitute here.’”
Judah said, “Let her keep it, lest we be shamed. Behold, I sent this young goat, and you haven’t found her.”

About three months later, Judah was told, “Tamar, your daughter-in-law, has played the prostitute. Moreover, behold, she is with child by prostitution.” Judah said, “Bring her out, and let her be burned.”

When she was brought out, she sent to her father-in-law, saying, “By the man, whose these are, I am with child.” She also said, “Please discern whose are these — the signet, and the cords, and the staff.”
Judah acknowledged them, and said, “She is more righteous than I, because I didn’t give her to Shelah, my son.” He knew her again no more.
In the time of her travail, behold, twins were in her womb.
When she travailed, one put out a hand, and the midwife took and tied a scarlet thread on his hand, saying, “This came out first.”
As he drew back his hand, behold, his brother came out, and she said, “Why have you made a breach for yourself?” Therefore his name was called Perez.
Afterward his brother came out, that had the scarlet thread on his hand, and his name was called Zerah.

footnotes.content: Judah goes down from his brothers and comes to Hirah, an Adullamite. Adullam sits in the lowland country west of the hill towns, and it will be remembered later as the place where David hid in a cave when he was hunted. Here it is simply where Judah leaves the family circle and begins to make his own way. I have watched how one step away from our people can become a long road, and how the Lord still follows us down it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah sees a Canaanite woman, the daughter of Shua, and takes her. The text says only that he saw her and went in to her — no counsel sought, no family consulted. It is the quiet beginning of a marriage that will shape the next chapters of his life. I have learned that what we do in a moment of looking can set the course of years.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She conceives and bears a son, and Judah names him Er. A firstborn son is a father's hope for the future, the name carried forward after him. Judah gives the boy a name in the land of his wandering rather than in the household of promise. Even our detours are not outside God's keeping.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She conceives again and bears a son, and this time she names him Onan. The woman who was taken without counsel now names her own child. Small details like this remind me that Scripture remembers the mothers too, and that God sees the ones the world passes over.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A third son is born, and she names him Shelah, and the text pauses to tell us Judah was at Chezib when he was born. Chezib lies in that same lowland country, a place so small we would not know it but for this line. God keeps His records in small places, with names we would otherwise forget.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah takes a wife for Er his firstborn, and her name is Tamar. We are told nothing of her father or her town; she enters the story as a woman given into this family. From here she will be the one who keeps faith with the family's duty while the men around her waver. I have often seen God's work carried by someone the story barely introduces.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Er, Judah's firstborn, is wicked in Yahweh's sight, and Yahweh kills him. The text does not tell us what his wickedness was, and I will not invent it. It simply says that God saw, and that God acted. That is a sober thing to write in a margin, and I write it on my knees.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah tells Onan to go in to his brother's wife and perform the duty of a husband's brother, to raise up offspring for Er. This is the levirate custom of that world, later written into Israel's law in Deuteronomy 25: a dead man's name and inheritance were kept alive through a child born to his widow. The custom is old, but the duty behind it is love — to give the dead their name and the widow her place. I think of One who did not count His own place too precious to give us His.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Onan knows the child would not be counted his, so he refuses to give his brother an heir, spilling the seed on the ground. The evil here is not one moment but a settled intent: he takes what belongs to the marriage while refusing its purpose, and defrauds both Tamar and his dead brother. I have seen how easy it is to keep the outward form of a duty while quietly withholding the heart of it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What Onan did was evil in Yahweh's sight, and God killed him also. Twice in a short space the text says that God saw and God acted. We do not like to speak of God's judgment, but a God who never judged would not be the God of the prophets or the psalms. The same hand that is severe here is the hand that will later bear judgment for us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah sends Tamar back to her father's house as a widow, telling her to wait until Shelah is grown, but the narrator lets us hear his real reason: he fears Shelah will die like his brothers. It is a promise made to be kept and quietly postponed. Tamar goes home and waits, and the years pass with no word. I have learned how much damage a kind tone can do when the promise behind it is not meant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah's wife, the daughter of Shua, dies, and when his mourning is eased he goes up to Timnah with his friend Hirah to shear his sheep. Shearing time was a season of work and feasting, a place to be among friends and to forget sorrow for a while. There is nothing wrong with comfort after grief. The trouble comes when comfort becomes the doorway to the next sin, as it will here.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Someone tells Tamar that her father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep. One sentence, passed along by an unnamed messenger, and it sets the rest of the story in motion. She has been waiting in her father's house, watching for a promise that never came. God's providence often turns on words carried by people who never knew what they carried.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tamar takes off her widow's garments, covers herself with a veil, and sits at the gate of Enaim on the road to Timnah, because she has seen that Shelah is grown and she was not given to him. The text is honest about her reasoning and does not dress it up. She is a woman with no advocate, using the only leverage she has. I find I cannot despise her here, and I notice that Scripture does not either.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah sees her and thinks she is a prostitute, because her face was covered. The veil that hid her from shame also hid her from recognition. He was not looking for a daughter-in-law; he was looking for what he wanted, and the covering let him see only that. How much of our sin begins with deciding in advance what we will not look at.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He turns aside to her and asks her to let him come in to her, not knowing she is his daughter-in-law. She answers with a question — what will you give me? She is not surprised by him; she has been waiting at this road. There is a strange sadness in the exchange: two people of the same family, bargaining in the dark, neither able to speak plainly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He promises a young goat from the flock, and she asks for a pledge until he sends it. She is thinking ahead; he is thinking only of the moment. It is the old difference between the one who must plan in order to survive and the one who can afford to forget. I have seen that difference in my own life more often than I care to admit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She asks for his signet, his cord, and the staff in his hand, and he gives them, and she conceives by him. These were no trifles: the signet was a man's personal seal, pressed into clay to bind his name to a promise, and the cord was what he wore it on. Judah handed over the very marks of who he was, and did not know it. Our pledges have a way of finding us again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She gets up, goes away, takes off the veil, and puts her widow's garments back on. In a few verses she is a widow again, and no one in her father's house knows what has happened. She carries the pledge and she carries a child, and she says nothing. Some people carry their whole case before God in silence, and He hears.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah sends the young goat by the hand of Hirah the Adullamite to get the pledge back, but Hirah does not find her. The goat was the price he had agreed to; it turns out to buy nothing. He cannot purchase back what he gave, and he cannot undo the night. There is a kindness even in this dead end, because it will not let him bury the truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hirah asks the men of the place where the prostitute is, the one at Enaim by the road, and they say there has never been a prostitute there. The woman he describes does not exist in that town. It is one of the quiet comedies of providence: the search is honest, the answer is honest, and the trail goes cold in God's hands. He knows how to keep a matter until the right day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hirah comes back and reports plainly: I did not find her, and the men of the place said there was no prostitute there. Two sentences, and the errand is closed. Judah's friend has done exactly what he was asked and no more. I notice that Hirah never asks the questions that would have embarrassed his friend, and I wonder how often I have been that kind of friend.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah says, let her keep it, lest we be shamed; I sent the goat and you did not find her. His concern is shame, not guilt. He would rather lose his seal and staff than have the matter talked about. I have known that trade — protecting a reputation while leaving the sin untouched — and I have learned it is a poor bargain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three months later Judah is told that Tamar has played the prostitute and is with child, and he says, bring her out and let her be burned. The man who went to a prostitute himself is quick to sentence the woman he thinks is one. The double standard is as old as Eden, and it is still with us. Yet the story is not finished, and the sentence is about to be interrupted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tamar is brought out, and she sends the signet, the cords, and the staff to her father-in-law with the words, please discern whose these are. The Hebrew word is the same one Judah used when he sent Joseph's bloodied coat to Jacob: please recognize. The man who asked his father to identify a garment is now asked to identify his own seal. God has a way of bringing us back to our own words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah acknowledges them and says, she is more righteous than I, because I did not give her to Shelah my son — and he knew her no more. This is the first confession in the story, and it comes from the guilty man, not the wronged one. Matthew's Gospel will later list Tamar among the mothers of Jesus (Matthew 1:3), a grace I would not have dared to write. He does not despise a contrite heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When her time comes, there are twins in her womb. After all the waiting, the bargaining, the fire sentence, and the confession, the story simply arrives at a birth. God is not embarrassed to build His next chapter out of a messy one. I have found that He often begins His best work where we are most ashamed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One of the twins puts out a hand, and the midwife ties a scarlet thread on it, saying, this one came out first. She does what midwives have always done, marking the firstborn so the rights and the records would be clear. A scarlet thread on a small wrist, tied by a woman whose name we never learn. God's purposes are often carried by hands like hers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But the hand draws back, the other brother comes out, and she says, why have you made a breach for yourself? So he is named Perez, which sounds like breach. The one marked first is not first after all, and the name of the moment becomes the name of the man. God's order frequently overturns ours, and He is not troubled by the reversal. This breach becomes a blessing, for Perez is in the line of David.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Afterward the brother with the scarlet thread on his hand comes out, and he is named Zerah. He wore the sign of the firstborn and still came second. Readers today hear an echo of that scarlet thread whenever a life is marked early by promise or by shame and then seems to arrive late. As of 2026-10, I am grateful that God's timing is not our lateness, and that He writes names we did not choose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
